slug: Dublin’s New Groove:  A review and interview of De Búrca at Whelans
title: Dublin’s New Groove:  A review and interview of De Búrca at Whelans
excerpt: “We need more experimentation. AI can't make weirdo fusion music.”
author: myc
body: De Búrca showcased their ability to dance a crowd through genres at their show in Whelans last Wednesday as an opening act for Henosis and Dog Swim. Rooted in funk, De Búrca performed syncopated bass rhythms from their bassist Gianni Filippeschi, dynamically played beside their in-the-pocket drummer Nathan Walsh. Gospel-like pianist Aleda Brady sang harmonies with their neo-soul guitarist and singer Leanna de Búrca. Self-described pop-funk band De Búrca opened the night and played like no one was watching, but it’s clear that they’re the ones to watch in the Dublin music scene.

When they spoke to us in an interview after the show, the band members shared how they bonded over the jazz-funk band Hiatus Kaiyote in a bar. Like De Búrca, Hiatus Kaiyote rarely stick to one genre, and in finding a shared love for the group’s music the 2nd year BIMM students who make up De Búrca “just clicked”. The self proclaimed genre-fluid nature of their music isn’t unfounded. When we caught up with the band after the show they listed influences of the likes of Remy Wolf, Billie Eilish, Vulfpeck, Jamiroquai, and of course Hiatus Kaiyote. Nathan stated, “Perrin Moss is just a phenomenal drummer”. As a band in the Dublin music scene De Búrca look up to the likes of Bricknasty and Avenue 68, another BIMM band, stating that “it'd be great to be on lineup with them”. De Búrca would like to see more funk bands coming up. They feel that Dublin needs more fusion, and to grow a bigger funk community. Bands noted by Nathan who are paving the way for funk in Ireland are the likes of Bricknasty and Grooveline: “They've kind of gone on to the next level”.

During De Búrca’s show they played a set of original songs and covered “Nakamarra” by Hiatus Kaiyote. For this cover Leanna handed her “De Búrca” rhinestone-embellished guitar to Oisín Reilly, a fellow BIMM student, to play as she sang and scatted across the stage. The cover was tastefully done and the group nailed the harmonies, but what stood out was the band's chemistry. Leanna wove through her band mates, engaging with them as she sang. The shared love for fusion music and Hiatus Kaiyote was clearly present on stage. When I commented on how great their chemistry on stage is, Leanna stated “I think just similar weird music tastes gel us together, honestly. I think we're all mates first as well.”

De Búrca’s original songs can only be described as fresh, which was scribbled in my notes multiple times during my attendance. Of what’s available on streaming their newest release “LOVE & REPEAT” is a great example of De Búrca’s pop influences. Never straying from the funk of the drum and bass, this song is full of consonant harmonies and the best example of De Búrca’s released music that captures their sound. Their song “Daffodil” takes new life on stage, full of scatting from Leanna with a Dolores O’Riordan tonality. Soft reverberated guitar, a strong funky bass groove alongside immaculately timed drums. With syncopated keys supporting consonant harmonies and raw emotional vocals. This is what made up the De Búrca sound in Whelans last Wednesday.

The band made it clear to the audience that “Train Song (Oh! My)” was a new song. A psych-funk blend, full of polyphonic melodies between Aleda’s orchestral keys and her shared pleasant harmonies with Leanna. This song was yet another brilliant example of the chemistry De Búrca had on stage with incredible presence from Leanna singing with such raw emotion, and the dynamic between their drummer Nathan and bassist Gianni as they continued to jam away.

“Washroom in Venus” is a song deeply entangled with femininity, with a fusion of R&B, neo-soul and alternative rock. The band never strayed away from a certain rhythmic groove reminiscent of Boa in their performance. Followed by “Poseidon” Aleda gave an enchanting vocal performance supported with keys and consonant harmonies from Leanna, leading into a drop and release of syncopated rhythm from the rest of the band.

When greeting De Búrca after their performance they apologised for a significant amount of “technical difficulties” during their 40 minute set. You wouldn’t have noticed. Their stage presence, engagement with the crowd, and ability to provide entertainment during frustrating alternative tunings covered any notable difficulties. Specifically during a rather prolonged tune up, Leanna thanked Ella-Marie Cullen of Henosis for inviting them to play, joking and laughing with the crowd and her bandmates that this was all a “trick for anticipation”. Saved by the kit, Nathan and Gianni followed by playing the viral math rock duo Angine de Poitrine’s “Sarniezz”. This song is of note as Angine de Poitrine is known for the complex structure of their songs that are inherently anti-AI. De Búrca mirrored this stance in our interview where Gianni stated, “We need more experimentation. AI can't make weirdo fusion music.”

When asked about their writing process they described their two very distinct methods. As Aleda and Leanna are both studying songwriting, Leanna stated in our interview that “we kind of have this way of delivering a basis of an idea to the band. But another method we have is these guys [Gianni and Nathan] getting something really cool rhythmically and then we build on that, I think that's where our better songs come from”. Following this Nathan countered that “I think it's just a different point of view” and that “you'll get a lot of weirder things” from Gianni and Nathan jamming. Making the point that because of this, they trust that “Leanne and Aleda are just gonna make it work, 'cause they have their point of views as songwriters, and actually writing songs. So they put a bit of a method to our madness.”

So what’s next for De Búrca? They plan to focus less on gigging or recording, and more on making their sound more solid and authentic. This plan is solidified by Leanna: “I think authenticity often gets lost in a lot of bands and songwriting, but I think once we define what we want to deliver to people as artists, then that would be really good for us”. Needless to say, whatever they're going to give us next will be full of groove and funk. As Nathan stated, “funk is better.”
Date of Show & interview: Wednesday May 6th 2026
